title: What is Orson Welles Best Film?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

Toss up between Kane and F For Fake for me.

Kane is an incredible milestone in cinema, and the greatest first film anyone’s ever made. Hard to believe he directed and starred in it at such a young age. I also feel like it stands up really well to time, both in terms of its message and techniques, which isn’t always true of films from the ‘30s.

I also think there’s incredible elements in Ambersons, Touch of Evil, The Trial, Chimes, Macbeth and Shanghai, but I would’ve say any of them can touch his other two.

But Fake is the one I’ve watched the most, and is so singular in terms of not just cinematic technique but also completely reinventing the documentary form into a kind of cinematic essay that is at once about art, storytelling, subjectivity, truth and most importantly, about Welles himself, that it’s kind of mind-boggling. No other artist could’ve made it, and for me that is the true mark of an auteur… that it springs almost fully formed from their id in a way that no one else could’ve birthed it.
I share your sentiment on F For Fake. Nobody else could have made that movie. It's so kinetic, so full of life and energy. The editing makes the film a masterpiece.

Kane is definitely in the conversation, and it's by far his most important film. That said, it took some studio interference to keep him from topping it with his very next film, and I think Welles continued to evolve as a director, so I hesitate to call Kane his *best* film.

Welles himself would have said Chimes at Midnight was his best, with The Trial coming in second. I can see why. Those are just less accessible films than Kane. In essence, they are deep cuts. It's easier to see how Kane, a much more "important" and flashy film, is ostentatiously "great".

It's hard to rank The Other Side of the Wind because he didn't finish it. It's high on the list for me, but it would have been higher had he finished it.

I'd say:

1. Chimes at Midnight
2. The Trial
3. Citizen Kane
4. The Magnificent Ambersons
5. Touch of Evil
6. The Other Side of the Wind
7. F for Fake
8. The Immortal Story
9. Othello
10. Macbeth
11. Mr. Arkadin
12. The Lady from Shanghai
13. The Stranger

Many argue that "F for Fake" is among the early mockumentaries, though there may have been contenders before it. It's tough to find any that match its impact, though. If that's true, then Orson Welles played a big part in popularizing this genre.

His best film, without a doubt, is Citizen Kane. The answer might be disappointing because of how predictable it is. What people often overlook, though, is how entertaining the film is even if you strip away all the technical innovations and non linear narratives.

I feel like terming it a “mockumentary” doesn’t fully encapsulate what it is, because mockumentaries are usually just presented as straight docos but everything is fabricated. Whereas this openly tells you stuff is fabricated, and even invites you into the editing room to experiment with the form.

I feel like it at times has more in common with the avant-garde movement and the early Soviet works of Vertov or Brakhage, than true documentary/mockumentary style.
I agree that it's incredibly entertaining even without all the flair. It could have been a great play.
I agree that there are many layers to the film. But there is one dominating aspect where Orson Wells clearly plays with aspects of truth and fiction.

I think they came up with the ending first, that they wanted the rich man to die alone.  And then they came up with the details to get to that point.

Since Hearst and none of the other inspirations for Kane (Welles included) actually wound up alone, it's not really particularly convincing to see it play out.  It's frankly a trillion to one shot that a Susan Alexander would walk away from a situation like that given what we saw.  Not authentic at all.

All of that says more about the bile of an alcoholic writer of the time, not that alcoholic writers were in particularly short supply back then.  It's something Mankiewicz wanted.  It wouldn't happen to someone like Kane unless he was mentally ill like Howard Hughes.

He really has three absolute masterpieces under his belt with 2 different genres of filmmaking and tv. His best fictional film is a toss up between Citizen Kane and the Immortal Story. Kane is absolutely a brilliant examination of a man who is enigmatic and defined by the perceived biases of the people that knew him. The way the story flows together is incredible for that particular time period— specifically the non-linear element which were rarely, if ever, used except for a few films like the Preston Sturges written Power of the Glory. The technical achievements he made in terms of deep focus, use of low angled lenses, ceilings, lighting techniques, and use of the soundtrack and overlapping dialogue is still innovative and impressive today. The Immortal Story is also a film I found more impressive in some ways because of how it deals with the fascination of mythological storytelling and the blending of reality and fiction, a theme that’s present through all of his work. The camerawork is surprisingly minimalist and being in color made me surprised at how great Welles was with color, and the characterization is absolutely on point and stunning.

In terms of documentary it has to be F for Fake. That film is one of the best edited films ever with how it intersects 6 different storylines yet cohesively puts it all together while playing a trick or two on the audience. Welles’ narration is pitch perfect and the tonality he brings propels the film forward at a lightning pace, and it’s so damn fun to watch that it’s endlessly rewatchable. The scene with him at the Notre Dame is still one of the most beautiful scenes in his entire filmography, just pure magic.

I would also recommend some of his tv documentary work like the pilot Portrait of Gena, which is an exploration into Italy and the culture surrounding it while also carrying the framework that F for Fake was built on and stuff that he carried over after doing his Peabody winning tv pilot, The Fountain of Youth.  Portrait of gena is available on YouTube if you want to check it out, and it is genuinely one of Welles’ all time best work imo. https://youtu.be/7LxyA4wxjdg?si=3qFo48ods3jJUvwV

Although Citizen Kane is not filmed theater at all

It's my favourite Welle's movie. Although Kane and Touch of Evil run it really close. They're all fantastic for very different reasons. 

Welle's was really disappointed that F flopped as he really thought he had invented something new with what he referred to as "the Cinematic Essay": a film both true and fictional at the same time. Not a documentary or a mockumentary, but an attempt to explore ideas and themes via a new audio/visual format. I personally think he was onto something and have often thought about creating something in this mode. Someone should return to it. The time is perfect right now.

There is a very good two-part BBC Arena documentary from the mid-80s wherein Welles discusses his whole career, including his love for F is For Fake. Well worth watching. If you're in the UK it's currently available on the iPlayer. Alongside a fantastic three-parter on Billy Wilder.

Oja Kodar is also sublimely beautiful.

Hughes was also a part inspiration for Kane though...
Admittedly, he was far from alone in 1940, but he did end up that way and in arguably a worse situation. Therefore, I'd argue that the ending does stack up. 

Actually watched Kane for the first time in over a decade last week on TV. A beautifully restored version that had lost none of it's freshness for me. The deep focus photography, the wit, the shot composition with its consistent "three sides to every story" visual motif, the symmetry of the intro and outro... 

 It's still a stunner for me and moves at a brisk pace for something approaching 85 years old. I think it's better, and infinitely more rewatchable, than Jeanne Dielman, 23 Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles. And at least equal to Vertigo (although all three are very different animals and comparing or ranking them is basically a fool's errand).

Obviously it's crazy to proclaim a "best film ever", but what would you personally place above Kane? Not a test or anything, I'm just genuinely curious as to what and why. I'm trying to think of contenders. I certainly wouldn't say Jeanne Dielman, 23 Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles was, to give the example of the current BFI choice. Vertigo has a shot for me, mind. 

What criteria do you think are best when ascertaining what constitutes greatness? Innovation? Structure? Technical brilliance? Performances? Themes? Longevity? Truth? Aesthetics? Purpose? Entertainment value? Depth? Conceit? Writing? Dialogue? 

All hypothetically speaking of course. I gave up ranking art just after I stopped having a favourite colour.

My personal pick is Lawrence of Arabia, but the brown face and lack of female characters make it a tough pick to recommend to people of color and women. That said! The breadth of the storytelling, combined with the nuance of character, THAT MUSIC, THOSE SHOTS.

And he's the most commercial director to also grasp for the unknown so regularly. 2001 is obvs a technical masterpiece; Barry Lyndon is another great Kubrick pick for Best Ever imo. 

​

What about you????

These are all solid choices. And I think amongst the overtly agreed pantheon it ultimately comes down to personal preference for personal reasons.

The aforementioned Vertigo has a strong shout for me: a noir in colour directorial confessional that also manages to work as an essay on the movies themselves as a whole. It's beautifully photographed, edited, scored, and performed. Even its poster is truly iconic - not in the bastardised usage of today. Its innovations are numerous - the first reverse zoom dolly for example. 

It also ages with you. On first viewing when young, the clockwork plot is what hooks. As you get older its complex psycho-sexual themes of obsession, the male gaze, deceit, neuroses, even masculinity itself, further reveal themselves with every viewing. It's a film about obsession that generates obsession, as its potential meanings continuosly flourish in an infinite regress of self-reflexive interpretation.

The story of its production is a meta-textual palimpsest in itself: the character of Madeleine represents Hitchcock's obsession with Grace Kelly and Vera Miles was set to play the role. However, she became pregnant and had to pull out resulting in Kim Novak taking over. So when Scottie first sees what he believes to be Madeleine in the museum that's Kim Novak replacing Vera Miles being Grace Kelly playing Judy pretending to be Madeleine who believes she's Carlotta Valdez.

See what I mean about "infinite regress"?

This is film that not only "entertains" as a thriller, it also rewards repeat viewing to peel back its layers - layers that use film itself to explore why we watch and who we choose to watch. Amongst many other things. But its no deliberately opaque modernist art film designed to deter the casual viewer and drag them through two hours of seemingly plotless esoteric image making. It's a blockbuster with big stars and tight plotting.

I get something new from it almost every time I see it. Which is probably every five years or so. There's not much that stands up like that.

As for some others I could, and have, happily waxed lyrically about for more than the average person could stand, I'd add:

Sorcerer - Friedkin's whip smart, nail biting and searingly anti-capitalist Apocalypse Now, which sadly suffered at the famous 77 fork in the road when George's space opera began the infantilisation of Hollywood in which we still find ourselves.

La Regle de Jeux - the premier country house as stand in for society murder flick comedy thriller satire. Set the template and rarely bettered.

Dr Strangelove - the blackest comedy of all time made at the height of the cold war with a pin-sharp, pitch perfect script and three of the greatest comedy performances of all time performed by one man in the same movie. As absurdly accurate regarding geopolitics today as it was then.

Les Quatre Cents Coups - a perfect slice of life from the perspective of a working class teenage boy alive with potential and affray whilst at play in one of the world's greatest cities. The promise, the problems, the possibilities...

L'eclisse - an achingly beautiful, infinitely examinable audio-visual poem to late-21st century middle class metropolitan ennui that you just want to climb inside and inhabit despite the aching desperation of its pretty unlikable characters. 

There's just so many contenders...

Also, Lyndon is a fine piece of work - especially technically. I finally saw it on the big screen in a beautiful 4K restoration with friends the other year. A magnificent beast I'd call it.

I'm curious as to your take on what places it as a contender though. Could you nutshell it for me? What is it about its themes that resonate personally for you? I find it a hard film to like. It's like it wants you to hate it. It's defiant, brutal and stand-offish - despite its obvious beauty - much like its protagonist and setting I suppose. It almost repels me.

If I want to watch a movie about Hughes, I'd watch The Aviator.  I'm not going to give Kane credit for something that hadn't happened yet.

For me, a lot of the enjoyment of the movie comes from story.  What do I think about these characters and this plot after the fact.  Not just watching the movie itself.  I downgrade Kane because I don't consider it that great a story.  Most of the Susan Alexander portion I just have no interest in, boring, unlikeable characters.  It's not King Lear or even Gone With The Wind.  It's a magic trick of a movie, an exercise in keeping balls in the air.  But it doesn't really mean anything as far as its story goes.  That matters to me.  People more interested in movie art for its own sake, cinematography, backstory of how the movie was made, go at it.  Story is a lot bigger piece for me.

Oof. I see you're brooking no dissent here, padre.

Well, I guess we'll have to just agree to disagree on this one. Appreciate your personal take even if I do vehemently disagree. I must say though that find your "analysis" a little myopic and overtly contrarian to be honest. And the "magic trick of a movie" line to be pithy but devoid of actual substance beyond a hollow leveraging of Welles' propensity towards literal stage magic. Storytelling is in and of itself a magic trick reliant on keeping many balls in the air. So not sure this is the pointed put down you believe it to be.

Beyond that, the screenplay and direction are pretty much universally highly regarded. So you're certainly sailing a lonely boat on this one in the grand scheme of things. But hey, horses for the proverbial as they say. You've got Welles and Mankiewicz down as bitter hacks and that's the hill you're prepared to expire on. Bold, iconoclastic, peculiar even, but perfectly fine in a subjective manner. 

Just to confirm though, am I right in thinking that for you story and likable protagonists are where the buck stops regarding movies? And technique and how those things are conveyed don't add much to the audience experience? Because that appears to be what you're saying and, if that's the case, you may prefer reading screenplays to watching movies.

Also, re: the Hughes ref - it's irrelevant that it hadn't yet happened in reality when justifying the supposed "realism" of the fictional denouement, because the fact that it did occur illustrates the distinct real-world possibility that it could. But I'm sure you realised that...

Frankly, The Aviator comment in general is a little bizarre. Kane is a composite roman a clef, not a biopic - the original title was American. You can't hold things responsible for not being what they're not supposed to be just because you want them to be something else.

In closing, it's absolutely fine that you didn't enjoy it. But your reasoning doesn't objectively stack up. For me.

Anyway, happy trails cowboy.
